newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China says debate of Hong Kong legislature closed.
newsitem.headline: China says debate of Hong Kong legislature closed.

text.p: China said on Friday that as far as it was concerned the debate over Hong Kong's provisional legislature -- the body set up by Beijing to run the territory after British rule ends this year -- was closed.
"This issue had been solved," Guo Chongli, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman, quoted Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen as saying in Singapore. "It's over. It's settled," he said.
Qian made the comments during one-and-a-half-hour talks with his British counterpart Malcolm Rifkind at a meeting of European and Asian foreign ministers.
Hong Kong will return to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

China has said it will scrap the territory's elected legislature after the handover and has already set up a new provisional legislature to set laws for the territory after sovereignty is transferred.
But Britain says the body breaks previous promises made by Beijing over the post-handover Hong Kong constitution.
Rifkind held out little prospect of China accepting criticism of Beijing's proposed interim constitution.
He had suggested in December that the International Court of Justice (World Court) in the Hague rule on the legality of the provisional legislature.
Rifkind said Qian had turned down this idea.
"The Chinese have not accepted the proposal," Rifkind told a news conference after meeting Qian. "Our suggestion remains on the table."
But the British Foreign Secretary said recent proposals to roll back some of the terms of Hong Kong's Bill of Rights and laws covering civil liberties may not be fully implemented.

"I certainly noted the clear statement by the foreign minister that China would not themselves seek to determine what should replace the (human rights) ordinances...that is for the chief executive designate and for the people of Hong Kong to decide," he said.
He said the man elected by a pro-Beijing committee to run Hong Kong under the Chinese, Tung Chee-hwa, was interested in consultations on the proposed changes.
"The consultations could at least reduce the damage caused by the repeal of these (civil rights) laws," Rifkind said.
Asked what value the meeting with Qian had been, he said: "The important point was to emphasise on a face-to-face basis...the very broad spectrum to what is being proposed on the human rights issue."
"These measures are very very foolish and very unwise," he said. "We strongly support the criticisms that have been made in Hong Kong of the establishment of the provisional legislature."
Qian said China was willing to keep the discussions over Hong Kong with Britain going.
"We do have different views, but disagreements can be solved through discussion and consultation," Guo quoted Qian as saying.
